planting.note: Best mounted or grown in shallow pots of coarse, fast-draining bark mix rather than garden soil; move outdoors only after nighttime lows hold above 55°F.

directions: This compact species earns its common name from the flattened, boat-shaped flower spike, which opens in overlapping segments of red and yellow that resemble a lobster's claw or a painted feather. Grow in bright, filtered light such as an east window or dappled patio shade, since direct midday sun scorches the soft foliage. Keep the central cup topped up with room-temperature water and flush it every couple of weeks to prevent stagnation, and mist occasionally in dry indoor air. After the rosette blooms it slowly declines, but pups form at the base and can be separated once they reach roughly a third the size of the parent for the next generation of plants.

planting.note: Pot in a loose, well-aerated epiphyte mix and keep out of any direct sun, which quickly bleaches the patterned foliage.

directions: Named for the fine crosswise mottling that overlays its broad, dark green leaves like a mosaic tile pattern, this understory species wants low, even light and steady warmth year-round. Keep the central cup filled with clean, low-mineral water and flush it regularly, since hard tap water can leave unsightly mineral spots on the pale leaf banding. Grow it in a fast-draining bark or fiber mix rather than heavy potting soil, and shield it from any drafts of cold or dry air. The eventual bloom is a compact head of white-pink bracts with short-lived white flowers, after which the rosette produces offsets that can be divided for propagation.

planting.note: Clumps readily into dense colonies outdoors in frost-free areas; elsewhere grow in containers of coarse, fast-draining mix and bring in before frost.

directions: The upright flower spike gives this species its common name, with slender pink bracts tipped in cobalt blue that look like a bundle of matchsticks held above the grey-green rosette. It tolerates brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit better than many bromeliads, making it a good choice for gardeners on the cooler edge of tropical zones. Grow in bright, filtered light or morning sun for the best flower color, and keep the central cup filled with water while letting the coarse potting mix dry slightly between waterings. It spreads readily by offsets into a multi-rosette clump, which can be divided every couple of years to refresh crowded plantings.

planting.note: Needs room to spread, as mature leaves can reach two feet or more; grow in large pots of chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix.

directions: This large-growing species is prized for its yellow-green leaves overlaid with a fine network of darker green veining, an effect that gives the foliage a translucent, window-paned look in bright indirect light. It is more shade-tolerant than most patterned vrieseas and actually loses its distinctive netting if exposed to strong direct sun. Keep the central cup filled with water and grow in a loose, chunky mix that drains quickly, since the wide rosette can trap excess moisture around its base if potted too densely. A tall, branched flower spike eventually rises from the center, and offsets that form afterward can be separated once well rooted.

planting.note: Forms tall, narrow tubular rosettes best appreciated at eye level on a stand, mount, or hanging basket.

directions: Distinctive silvery cross-banding gives this tall, tubular billbergia its zebra-striped look, and mature clumps send out arching stalks of pendant chartreuse and pink flowers edged in blue that dangle below the foliage. Like other billbergias it shrugs off short cold snaps better than most bromeliads and can handle a bit more direct morning sun without scorching. Keep the tight central tube topped up with water, let the coarse potting mix dry slightly between waterings, and mount or pot it where the pendant blooms can hang freely for viewing. Offsets form readily at the base and can be separated to build new clumps.

planting.note: A classic mid-century hybrid best grown in a hanging basket or elevated container so the pendant flower stalk can be seen from below.

directions: Bred by pioneering bromeliad hybridizer Mulford Foster, this enduringly popular cultivar forms a smooth rosette of glossy, wine-red leaves that darken further with brighter light. Its drooping flower stalk carries small blue-tipped flowers followed by long-lasting coral-red berries that give the plant extra seasonal interest well after bloom. Grow in bright, filtered light with the central cup kept filled with water, and use a coarse, fast-draining bromeliad mix since the roots are mainly for anchorage rather than uptake. Established rosettes send out several pups at the base, which can be divided once they have their own root systems.
